Let $u$ be an almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable functions on
$\mathbb R$ with $u\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$,
using the quotient convention of
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], the essentially bounded
class of [[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]], and the local integrability
convention of [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]. For $h>0$ define
$$D_hu(x):=u(x+h)-u(x),\qquad \operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u):=\sup_{h>0}\frac1h\int_{\mathbb R}|D_hu(x)|\,dx,$$
where the integral may be $+\infty$. The **bounded BV class on the line**
$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ consists of those classes for which
$\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u)<\infty$; we write
$\operatorname{TV}(u):=\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u)$.

This translation-variation convention is the standard one-dimensional BV
seminorm on bounded locally integrable classes. It is unchanged by modifying
$u$ on a null set, because each translate of a null set is null. It does not
require $u\in L^1(\mathbb R)$: every bounded constant function belongs to
$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and has variation $0$.

If $a$ or $c$ increases, monotonicity of $F$ in its first or second coordinate makes $H$ nondecreasing in that variable. Let $S$ denote the sequence update. If $x,y\in I^{\mathbb Z}$ and $\sum_j|x_j-y_j|<\infty$, monotonicity gives $|Sx-Sy|\le S(x\vee y)-S(x\wedge y)$ coordinatewise. For any $z,w$ with $\sum_j|z_j-w_j|<\infty$, summing the update over $-N\le j\le N$ yields $\sum_{j=-N}^N(Sz_j-Sw_j)=\sum_{j=-N}^N(z_j-w_j)-\lambda(d_N-d_{-N-1}),\quad d_j:=F(z_j,z_{j+1})-F(w_j,w_{j+1}).$ The coordinate Lipschitz bounds make $\sum_j|d_j|<\infty$, so both boundary terms tend to zero. The update difference is absolutely summable, and hence $\sum_j(Sz_j-Sw_j)=\sum_j(z_j-w_j)$. Applying this to $z=x\vee y$ and $w=x\wedge y$ proves $\|Sx-Sy\|_1\le\|x-y\|_1$.

The initial neighbor difference is summable by step 1.1. The update commutes with integer shifts because the same $H$ is applied at every index. Let $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and put $V:=\operatorname{TV}(u_0)$.
Let $U^n=(U_j^n)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ be generated by
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]] under its full invariant-interval
CFL bound. Define the update map
$$H(a,b,c):=b-\lambda\bigl(F(b,c)-F(a,b)\bigr).$$
Then $H$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate on $I^3$ and $H(s,s,s)=s$ for
$s\in I$. Consequently,
$$a_-\le U_j^n\le a_+\quad(j\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge0),\qquad \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n|\le V\quad(n\ge0).$$
Moreover, for every $n\ge0$,
$$\frac h\tau\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|\le (L_1+L_2)V.$$
For a sequence $x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$, the notation
$\|x\|_1:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|x_j|$ is used only when this sum is finite;
$x\vee y$ and $x\wedge y$ mean the coordinatewise maximum and minimum.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$, and
$\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. The unknown and initial datum are equivalence
classes $[u]\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)$ and
$[u_0]\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, where
equality is Lebesgue-a.e. ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).

For $k\in\mathbb R$ define the **Kruzhkov entropy pair**
$$\eta_k(s)=|s-k|,\qquad q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)\bigl(f(s)-f(k)\bigr),$$
with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then $\eta_k$ is convex
and $q_k'=\eta_k'f'$ almost everywhere, so $(\eta_k,q_k)$ is a locally Lipschitz convex
entropy--entropy flux pair ([[def-convex-entropy-entropy-flux-pair]]).

The class $[u]$ is a **Kruzhkov entropy solution** of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with initial trace $[u_0]$ if:

(i) for every $k\in\mathbb R$ and every nonnegative
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Pi_T)$,
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\bigl(\eta_k(u)\,\varphi_t+q_k(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\ge0,$$
that is, $\partial_t\eta_k(u)+\operatorname{div}_x q_k(u)\le0$ in
$\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$; and

(ii) for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{0<t<\min\{\delta,T\}}\int_K|u(t,x)-u_0(x)|\,dx=0.$$

The integral in (i) is independent of the representative because its integrand
is unchanged almost everywhere. For (ii), Fubini's theorem gives locally
integrable spatial sections for almost every $t$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the
displayed slice integral is defined for those times and its essential supremum
ignores the exceptional null set. If $u$ or $u_0$ is changed on a null set in
its respective space, Fubini's theorem shows that the slice-integral function
changes only for a null set of times, so the trace condition is well defined on
the equivalence classes: this is the **strong local $L^1$ initial trace**.

Taking $k$ above and below the essential range of $u$ makes $\eta_k$ equal
$k-u$ and $u-k$, whose $t$- and $x$-derivatives cancel the constant terms
against compactly supported test functions, so the entropy inequalities imply
the weak conservation law of
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]] tested
against nonnegative test functions, hence by linearity against all test
functions.

To recover the Cauchy boundary term, apply the interior weak identity to
$\varphi(t,x)\zeta(t/\delta)$, where $\zeta$ is smooth and nondecreasing,
$\zeta=0$ on $(-\infty,1/2]$ and $\zeta=1$ on $[1,\infty)$.
For $\delta>0$ this product is supported away from $t=0$, so it is
an admissible interior test. The term containing $\zeta'/\delta$
converges to $\int u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx$ by (ii), while the other terms
converge on the compact support. This proves the full weak formulation with
initial datum $u_0$, rather than only its interior equation.

derivations.claim: If $s\ge k$, then $s\vee k=s$ and $s\wedge k=k$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(s)-f(k)=q_k(s)$. If $s<k$, then $s\vee k=k$ and $s\wedge k=s$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(k)-f(s)=q_k(s)$.

First suppose $k\in I$. Put $X=(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$ and let $X^+$ and $X^-$ be its coordinatewise maximum and minimum with $(k,k,k)$. Both triples lie in $I^3$. By [F1], the two numbers $H(X)$ and $H(k,k,k)=k$ lie between $H(X^-)$ and $H(X^+)$; therefore $|H(X)-k|\le H(X^+)-H(X^-).$ Expanding the definition of $H$, the right side is $|U_j^n-k|-\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr),$ which gives the claimed inequality after rearrangement.

If $k<a_-$, every state is above $k$ by the range assertion in [F1]. Then $|U_j^n-k|=U_j^n-k$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(a,b)-F(k,k)$ for state pairs; substituting the scheme recurrence makes the displayed left side zero. If $k>a_+$, every state is below $k$, so $|U_j^n-k|=k-U_j^n$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(k,k)-F(a,b)$; substitution again gives zero. The cases $k=a_-$ and $k=a_+$ are already covered by step 2.1.

$$H(a,b,c):=b-\lambda\bigl(F(b,c)-F(a,b)\bigr).$$

Let $U_j^n$ be the states on a mesh from
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], with cell-time slabs
$I_j\times[t_n,t_{n+1})$ and $t_n=n\tau$. The **piecewise-linear time

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For every $t$, $W_m(\cdot,t)$ is piecewise constant with values in $I$ and spatial variation at most $V$: on each time slab it is a convex combination of two states whose variations are at most $V$ by [F2]. Here the variation of a piecewise-constant section on an interval is the sum of the absolute jump sizes inside that interval. Fix an integer $R\ge1$ and consider any sequence $v_m$ of such sections on $[-R,R]$. At each rational point in $[-R,R]$, the values lie in the compact interval $I$. The bounded-value subsequence at one rational point exists by [F6]; explicitly, partition $I$ into finitely many closed intervals of length at most $2^{-1}$, take the first interval containing infinitely many values, and repeat inside it with successive meshes $2^{-2},2^{-3},\ldots$, always selecting the first subinterval with infinitely many retained indices. The nested intervals have diameters tending to zero, so the least increasing indices in the nested sets give a convergent subsequence. Enumerate the rationals in $[-R,R]$ and repeat this deterministic extraction successively on the current subsequence. The nested subsequences yield a diagonal subsequence converging at every rational point; each interval and index is selected by a least-index rule, so this uses no choice axiom. Given $\delta>0$, choose a finite rational partition of $[-R,R]$ with mesh at most $\delta$, possible by [F4]. For each subinterval $J=[r_i,r_{i+1}]$ and any two selected functions $v_p,v_q$, variation gives $|v_p(x)-v_q(x)|\le|v_p(r_i)-v_q(r_i)|+\operatorname{Var}_J(v_p)+\operatorname{Var}_J(v_q)$ for almost every $x\in J$. Integrating and summing yields $\|v_p-v_q\|_{L^1([-R,R])}\le 2\delta V+2R\max_i|v_p(r_i)-v_q(r_i)|.$ For the fixed partition the maximum tends to zero as $p,q\to\infty$; then taking $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the selected sections are Cauchy in local $L^1$.

On each slab, $\partial_tW_m=(U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n)/\tau_m$ on cell $I_j$. By [F2], its $L^1(\mathbb R)$ norm is at most $C:=(L_1+L_2)V$. Integrating over any time interval gives $\|W_m(\cdot,t)-W_m(\cdot,s)\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\le C|t-s|.$ Enumerate the rational times in $[0,T]$ and the integer intervals $[-R,R]$, which are countable by [F5]. Apply step 1.1 successively at each rational time and take a diagonal subsequence using its least-indexed bisection choices. The subsequence converges in $L^1([-R,R])$ at every rational time for every integer $R$; this recursive construction uses no choice axiom.

Fix $R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a finite set of rational times whose consecutive gaps are less than $\varepsilon/(4(C+1))$, possible by [F4]. At those finitely many times the subsequence in step 2.1 is Cauchy in $L^1([-R,R])$. For any $t\in[0,T]$, choose a net time $s$ within the gap bound; the triangle inequality and the uniform time estimate in step 2.1 give $\|W_p(\cdot,t)-W_q(\cdot,t)\|_{L^1([-R,R])}\le 2C|t-s|+\|W_p(\cdot,s)-W_q(\cdot,s)\|_{L^1([-R,R])}.$ Thus the subsequence is uniformly Cauchy in time in local $L^1$. For fixed $t,R$, its bounded measurable sections have an $L^1([-R,R])$ limit: for each $j$, let $N_j$ be the least integer such that all $p,q\ge N_j$ have $L^1([-R,R])$ difference below $2^{-j}$, which exists by Cauchyness; recursively choose the least increasing indices $n_j\ge N_j$. Then successive differences have norms below $2^{-j}$, so [F8] makes their pointwise absolute sum finite almost everywhere, and dominated convergence [F7] gives the $L^1$ limit. Uniqueness makes these limits consistent as $R$ increases, and the uniform Cauchy estimate makes $t\mapsto u(t)$ continuous in each local $L^1$ norm. The subsequence is also Cauchy in $L^1([-R,R]\times(0,T))$ for every integer $R$, by integrating its uniform-in-time Cauchy bound. For each $j$, let $M_j$ be the least integer such that all $p,q\ge M_j$ have difference below $2^{-j}$ on every cylinder with integer $R\le j$; this exists because there are finitely many such cylinders and the sequence is Cauchy on each. Recursively choose the least increasing indices $m_j\ge M_j$. Their successive differences have norm below $2^{-j}$ on every such cylinder. [F8] then gives a finite pointwise sum of differences almost everywhere on each cylinder, and [F7] yields a measurable space-time limit with strong local $L^1$ convergence. Finally [F9] identifies its sections with the continuous local-$L^1$ limits for almost every time.

Every $W_m$ takes values in $I$, so its local $L^1$ limit also takes values in $I$ almost everywhere: if, for example, $u(t)>a_+$ on a set of positive measure, then some set where $u(t)\ge a_++1/r$ has positive measure, contradicting $L^1$ convergence from functions bounded by $a_+$. The same argument applies to the lower bound.

For $r<0$, translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives the same bound as for $-r$, so $\|u_0(\cdot+r)-u_0\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\le |r|V$ for every $r\in\mathbb R$. On each cell, the initial cell-average error is controlled by translations: $\sum_j\int_{I_j}|u_0(x)-U_j^0|\,dx\le\frac1h\int_{-h}^{h}\int_{\mathbb R}|u_0(x+r)-u_0(x)|\,dx\,dr\le hV.$ The first inequality follows by writing each cell average as an integral over that same cell, applying the triangle inequality, and changing variables to $r=y-x$; the restriction that $x$ and $x+r$ lie in the same cell can only decrease the integral. Since $W_m(\cdot,0)=U^0$, step 3.1 gives $u(0)=u_0$ in local $L^1$.

On each slab, $|W_m-U_j^n|=\theta|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|$. Integrating in time contributes the factor $\tau_m/2$; the time-increment bound in [F2] gives, on $[0,T]$, $\|W_m-\mathcal U_m\|_{L^1(\mathbb R\times(0,T))}\le\frac{(T+\tau_m)\tau_m}{2}(L_1+L_2)V\longrightarrow0.$ Consequently $\mathcal U_m$ converges strongly in local space-time $L^1$ to the same limit as $W_m$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $U_j^n$ be the states on a mesh from
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], with cell-time slabs
$I_j\times[t_n,t_{n+1})$ and $t_n=n\tau$. The **piecewise-linear time
interpolant** $W_{h,\tau}$ is constant in $x$ on each cell and, for
$t\in[t_n,t_{n+1})$, is
$$W_{h,\tau}(x,t):=(1-\theta)U_j^n+\theta U_j^{n+1},\qquad \theta:=\frac{t-t_n}{\tau},\qquad x\in I_j.$$
The piecewise-constant state $\mathcal U_{h,\tau}$ and face flux
$\mathcal Q_{h,\tau}$ use the convention of
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]]. Values on mesh boundaries
are irrelevant to the corresponding Lebesgue classes.

The interpolant is affine in time on each slab and has the scheme values at
both time endpoints. Its purpose here is to obtain time-uniform local compactness
and the strong initial trace; the weak-limit supplier is applied to
$\mathcal U_{h,\tau}$ after proving that the two reconstructions have the same
strong local limit.

Let $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and put $V:=\operatorname{TV}(u_0)$.
Let $U^n=(U_j^n)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ be generated by
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]] under its full invariant-interval
CFL bound. Define the update map
$$H(a,b,c):=b-\lambda\bigl(F(b,c)-F(a,b)\bigr).$$
Then $H$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate on $I^3$ and $H(s,s,s)=s$ for
$s\in I$. Consequently,
$$a_-\le U_j^n\le a_+\quad(j\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge0),\qquad \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n|\le V\quad(n\ge0).$$
Moreover, for every $n\ge0$,
$$\frac h\tau\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|\le (L_1+L_2)V.$$
For a sequence $x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$, the notation
$\|x\|_1:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|x_j|$ is used only when this sum is finite;
$x\vee y$ and $x\wedge y$ mean the coordinatewise maximum and minimum.

Let $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ with $V=\operatorname{TV}(u_0)$ and
$I=[a_-,a_+]$. Let $(h_m,\tau_m)$ satisfy $h_m,\tau_m\to0$ and the full
invariant-interval CFL bound for the scheme of
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]]. Let $W_m$ and $\mathcal U_m$ be
the piecewise-linear and piecewise-constant reconstructions of
[[def-piecewise-linear-fv-time-interpolant]]. Then every subsequence has a
further subsequence for which $W_m$ converges uniformly in time in
$L^1(K)$ on every bounded interval $K\subset\mathbb R$ to a map
$t\mapsto u(t)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, continuous in local $L^1$,
with $u(0)=u_0$ and $a_-\le u(t)\le a_+$ almost everywhere. On that subsequence
the piecewise-constant reconstructions converge strongly to the same $u$ in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $T>0$, $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, and $F\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $F(a,a)=f(a)$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $m$, form the conservative finite-volume scheme and space-time reconstruction of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]] and [[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] using $h_m,\tau_m\to0$ and initial cell averages of $u_0$. Suppose reconstructions converge strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$ to $u$, and for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is $M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on $I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution in the sense of [[def-locally-bounded-distributional-weak-solution]]; explicitly, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.
$$
The strong convergence and local uniform bounds are hypotheses, not conclusions. No CFL condition or entropy inequality is assumed, so the theorem proves a weak limit only; it does not claim Kruzhkov entropy admissibility. If the limit is also globally essentially bounded, this identity is the published bounded weak formulation in [[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]].

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$, and
$\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. The unknown and initial datum are equivalence
classes $[u]\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)$ and
$[u_0]\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, where
equality is Lebesgue-a.e. ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).

For $k\in\mathbb R$ define the **Kruzhkov entropy pair**
$$\eta_k(s)=|s-k|,\qquad q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)\bigl(f(s)-f(k)\bigr),$$
with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then $\eta_k$ is convex
and $q_k'=\eta_k'f'$ almost everywhere, so $(\eta_k,q_k)$ is a locally Lipschitz convex
entropy--entropy flux pair ([[def-convex-entropy-entropy-flux-pair]]).

The class $[u]$ is a **Kruzhkov entropy solution** of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with initial trace $[u_0]$ if:

(i) for every $k\in\mathbb R$ and every nonnegative
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Pi_T)$,
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\bigl(\eta_k(u)\,\varphi_t+q_k(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\ge0,$$
that is, $\partial_t\eta_k(u)+\operatorname{div}_x q_k(u)\le0$ in
$\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$; and

(ii) for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{0<t<\min\{\delta,T\}}\int_K|u(t,x)-u_0(x)|\,dx=0.$$

The integral in (i) is independent of the representative because its integrand
is unchanged almost everywhere. For (ii), Fubini's theorem gives locally
integrable spatial sections for almost every $t$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the
displayed slice integral is defined for those times and its essential supremum
ignores the exceptional null set. If $u$ or $u_0$ is changed on a null set in
its respective space, Fubini's theorem shows that the slice-integral function
changes only for a null set of times, so the trace condition is well defined on
the equivalence classes: this is the **strong local $L^1$ initial trace**.

Taking $k$ above and below the essential range of $u$ makes $\eta_k$ equal
$k-u$ and $u-k$, whose $t$- and $x$-derivatives cancel the constant terms
against compactly supported test functions, so the entropy inequalities imply
the weak conservation law of
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]] tested
against nonnegative test functions, hence by linearity against all test
functions.

To recover the Cauchy boundary term, apply the interior weak identity to
$\varphi(t,x)\zeta(t/\delta)$, where $\zeta$ is smooth and nondecreasing,
$\zeta=0$ on $(-\infty,1/2]$ and $\zeta=1$ on $[1,\infty)$.
For $\delta>0$ this product is supported away from $t=0$, so it is
an admissible interior test. The term containing $\zeta'/\delta$
converges to $\int u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx$ by (ii), while the other terms
converge on the compact support. This proves the full weak formulation with
initial datum $u_0$, rather than only its interior equation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, and $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$
be $C^1$. Let $M,L\ge0$ and assume $|f(a)-f(b)|\le L|a-b|$ for all
$a,b\in[-M,M]$. Let $u,v$ be bounded Kruzhkov entropy solutions on $\Pi_T$ in
the sense of [[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]], with $|u|,|v|\le M$ almost
everywhere and initial data $u_0,v_0\in L^\infty\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. For
each fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $R>0$, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$
satisfying $Lt<R$,
$$\int_{B(x_0,R-Lt)}|u(t,x)-v(t,x)|\,dx\le\int_{B(x_0,R)}|u_0(x)-v_0(x)|\,dx.$$
In particular, for each fixed $x_0,R$, if $u_0=v_0$ almost everywhere on
$B(x_0,R)$, then $u(t,\cdot)=v(t,\cdot)$ almost everywhere on $B(x_0,R-Lt)$ for
almost every $t$ with $Lt<R$. The exceptional null set may depend on $x_0$ and
$R$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the heat-kernel, $L^1$ completeness and
vanishing-viscosity extraction interfaces used below. Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, let
$f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be locally Lipschitz and $C^1$, and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^n)$. Then there exists a
Kruzhkov entropy solution
$u\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)\cap C^0([0,T];L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n))$ of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$ in the strong
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ sense, satisfying $\|u(t,\cdot)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty$
for every $t$. By
[[cor-uniqueness-comparison-and-order-preservation-for-entropy-solutions]] this
solution is unique. The route is vanishing viscosity, and the compactness comes
from the translation lemmas, not from the energy dissipation alone
([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]], [[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]).

Let $U^n$ be a scheme from
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], satisfying the full
invariant-interval CFL bound. For $k\in\mathbb R$ define
$$G_k(a,b):=F(a\vee k,b\vee k)-F(a\wedge k,b\wedge k),\qquad q_k(s):=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)(f(s)-f(k)),$$
where $q_k$ is the Kruzhkov entropy flux of
[[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]. Then $G_k(s,s)=q_k(s)$ for every $s\in I$,
and for every $j\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$,
$$|U_j^{n+1}-k|-|U_j^n-k|+\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr)\le0.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Start with any subsequence of meshes. By [F4] it has a further subsequence along which $W_m$ converges in $C([0,T];L^1_{\mathrm{loc}})$ to a map $u(t)$ with $u(0)=u_0$, values in $I$, and $\mathcal U_m\to u$ strongly in space-time $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The range condition gives the uniform local state bound required below.

Fix $k\in\mathbb R$ and a nonnegative $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$. Let $\Phi_j^n$ be the average of $\varphi$ on $I_j\times[t_n,t_{n+1}]$, and choose $N$ so that $\varphi$ vanishes on and after the last time slab. Multiply the one-step inequality [F9] by $h\Phi_j^n$, sum over the finitely many relevant $j,n$, telescope in time, and reindex the shared entropy fluxes in space. The resulting exact inequality is $\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\sum_j h|U_j^n-k|(\Phi_j^n-\Phi_j^{n-1})+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_j\tau G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)(\Phi_{j+1}^n-\Phi_j^n)\ge0.$ There is no initial term because $\varphi$ is supported away from $t=0$.

The hypotheses of [F5] hold along this further subsequence: $f$ is continuous, the cell data and shared-flux recurrence are those of [F1], the mesh widths vanish, the states are bounded by $I$, and the strong local convergence is from step 1.1. Therefore $u$ satisfies the distributional weak equation with the prescribed initial boundary term.

On the compact state interval $J$ spanned by $I\cup\{k\}$, local Lipschitz continuity of $F$ gives a finite constant $C_k$ for which $|G_k(a,b)-G_k(a,a)|\le C_k|b-a|$. By [F3], the local space-time $L^1$ difference between the face entropy flux $G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$ and $q_k(U_j^n)=G_k(U_j^n,U_j^n)$ is at most $C_k T h_m\operatorname{TV}(u_0)$, which tends to zero. Also $q_k$ is Lipschitz on $I$ because $f\in C^1$, so strong convergence in step 1.1 gives $q_k(\mathcal U_m)\to q_k(u)$ in local $L^1$.

The finite-sum expression in step 1.2 converges to $\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(|u-k|\varphi_t+q_k(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt.$ Writing $\overline{\varphi_t}{}_j^n$ for the average of $\varphi_t$ on $I_j\times[t_n,t_{n+1}]$, Taylor's formula in time gives $|\Phi_j^n-\Phi_j^{n-1}-\tau_m\overline{\varphi_t}{}_j^n|\le C_\varphi\tau_m^2$. After multiplication by $h_m|U_j^n-k|$ and summing the $O(h_m^{-1})$ cells and $O(\tau_m^{-1})$ slabs in the compact support, the error is $O(\tau_m)$. For the flux term, translation of adjacent cell averages gives $\tau_m(\Phi_{j+1}^n-\Phi_j^n)=\int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}\int_{I_j}h_m^{-1}\int_0^{h_m}\varphi_x(x+s,t)\,ds\,dx\,dt$; replacing the averaged derivative by $\varphi_x$ has total error $O(h_m)$ because $\varphi_{xx}$ and the numerical entropy fluxes are uniformly bounded on the compact support. The face-flux replacement in step 2.2 and strong state convergence supply the remaining limit. Passing to the limit in step 1.2 proves the Kruzhkov inequality for this $k,\varphi$. Since both were arbitrary, all interior Kruzhkov inequalities hold.

The initial value and continuity from [F4] imply the strong local $L^1$ trace: for every compact interval $K$, $\|u(t)-u_0\|_{L^1(K)}\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, hence the essential supremum over $0<t<\delta$ also tends to zero. Together with the entropy inequalities of step 3.1, [F6] makes $u$ a bounded Kruzhkov entropy solution.

Put $M_0:=\max\{|a_-|,|a_+|\}$. By [F10], $f$ is Lipschitz on $[-M_0,M_0]$, which contains the range $I$ of every limit from step 4.1. Thus the range and flux hypotheses of [F7] hold for any pair of such limits. If $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, [A2] and [F8] supply a bounded Kruzhkov solution, and [F7] makes it unique and identifies it with the limit of step 4.1. If $u_0\notin L^1(\mathbb R)$, step 4.1 itself supplies existence and [F7] supplies uniqueness. Thus in either branch there is a unique target entropy solution, without applying the global existence theorem outside its $L^1$ domain.

Every convergent subsequence from step 1.1 has an entropy-solution limit with the same initial data; by [F7] all such limits agree with the unique target from step 5.1. If the full sequence failed to converge strongly on some compact space-time set, a subsequence would stay at distance at least $\varepsilon>0$ from that target; [F4] would give a further subsequence converging strongly there to an entropy solution, contradicting uniqueness. Therefore $\mathcal U_m\to u$ strongly in local space-time $L^1$. Uniform-in-time local convergence of $W_m$ follows by the same subsequence contradiction using [F4].

function $u\colon\mathbb R\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R$ is a **locally bounded
distributional weak solution** of $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ with initial datum $u_0$ if
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and every $T'<T$ it is
essentially bounded on $I\times(0,T')$, and, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$ \int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0. $$
The integrals are local: if a test is supported in $I\times[-S,T']$ with $I$
bounded and $T'<T$, the local essential bound makes $u$ bounded on

range. The initial integral is finite because $u_0$ is locally integrable and
$\varphi(\cdot,0)$ is compactly supported. This is the local
integrability version of the weak identity in
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]], whose
published formulation assumes a global $L^\infty$ bound. This definition adds
no entropy inequality or strong local $L^1$ trace requirement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed

the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there

be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For Burgers' flux $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, define $G\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ as follows. If $a\le b$, set
$$ G(a,b)=\begin{cases} a^2/2,&a\ge0,\\ b^2/2,&a<0\text{ and }b\le0,\\ 0,&a<0<b. \end{cases} $$ If $b<a$, set $$ G(a,b)=\frac12\max\{a^2,b^2\}. $$
This is the Godunov flux for the convex Burgers flux: for increasing states it
uses the minimum of $f_B$ on $[a,b]$, and for decreasing states it uses the
maximum of $f_B$ on $[b,a]$. It is proposed as a particular numerical flux in
the scheme of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Its continuity and
consistency are verified in the pair.

The map $G$ defined in [[def-godunov-flux-for-burgers]] is continuous on
$\mathbb R^2$ and satisfies $G(a,a)=f_B(a)=a^2/2$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and also assume Dependent Choice $\mathrm{DC}$ if $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb R)$. Let $f_B(s)=s^2/2$ and use the Godunov flux $G$ of
[[def-godunov-flux-for-burgers]]. For every compact invariant interval $I\subseteq[-M,M]$
with $M>0$, the two coordinate Lipschitz bounds can be taken to be
$L_1=L_2=M$, and $G$ is nondecreasing in its first argument and nonincreasing
in its second. Therefore, for any $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ with values
in $I$, every mesh family satisfying
$$\frac{\tau_m}{h_m}\le\frac1{2M},\qquad \frac{\tau_m}{h_m}\ge c_*>0,\qquad h_m,\tau_m\to0$$
falls under [[thm-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-convergence]] and converges
strongly locally to the unique Burgers entropy solution.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $T>0$,
$f\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, and $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ in the sense of
[[def-bounded-bv-data-on-line]]. Put
$I=[\operatorname*{ess\,inf}u_0,\operatorname*{ess\,sup}u_0]$. Let
$F\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz, consistent with $f$,
nondecreasing in its first coordinate and nonincreasing in its second on
$I^2$, with coordinate Lipschitz bounds $L_1,L_2$ as in
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]]. For a family of meshes
$(h_m,\tau_m)$ assume
$$h_m,\tau_m\to0,\qquad \frac{\tau_m}{h_m}(L_1+L_2)\le1,\qquad \frac{\tau_m}{h_m}\ge c_*>0.$$
For each mesh, initialize by cell averages and update with the shared flux $F$.
Let $W_m$ be the piecewise-linear time interpolant and $\mathcal U_m$ the
piecewise-constant state reconstruction. If $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, assume
Dependent Choice $\mathrm{DC}$ in addition to $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; no DC
assumption is made when $u_0\notin L^1(\mathbb R)$.

Then there is a unique bounded Kruzhkov entropy solution $u$ on
$\mathbb R\times(0,T)$ with initial datum $u_0$, and
$$W_m\longrightarrow u\quad\text{in }C([0,T];L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)),\qquad \mathcal U_m\longrightarrow u\quad\text{strongly in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T)).$$
For nonintegrable bounded BV data, existence is obtained from the local
finite-volume limit in the proof before local contraction gives uniqueness.
The theorem claims local convergence; global $L^1$ convergence requires
additional uniform tail control. The time-to-space lower bound $c_*$ is retained
from the approved convergence interface, and no system-valued or non-BV
entropy-process conclusion is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, let
$f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. A bounded
measurable $u\colon\Pi_T\to\mathbb R$ is a **distributional weak solution** of
the Cauchy problem $u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$, if for
every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n\times(-\infty,T))$ --- test functions
whose support may meet the initial plane $t=0$ --- one has
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\Bigl(u\,\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\Bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$
Equivalently $u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$, together
with the displayed initial boundary term
([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). The integrals are absolutely
convergent: $u$ is bounded, $f(u)$ is bounded on the bounded range of $u$, and
$\varphi$ has compact support, so the pairings are $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ pairings
and are representative-independent ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]; the product-space identities
are those of [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and
[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]). The condition is an
equality in the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ classes of $u$ and $f(u)$; it involves no
pointwise assignment of $u$ on $\{t=0\}$, and the initial datum enters only
through the boundary term ([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]]). For the
entropy formulation of this page the initial condition is instead imposed as a
strong local $L^1$ trace ([[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]).

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$
([[def-scalar-conservation-law-and-flux]]), and let $u$ be a piecewise $C^1$
distributional weak solution
([[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]]) with
two-sided $C^1$ interface $\Gamma$ and traces as in
[[def-piecewise-smooth-shock-and-one-sided-traces]]. Orient the unit
space--time normal $\nu=(\nu_t,\nu_x)$ from the minus side to the plus side.
Then at every $\zeta\in\Gamma\subset U$,
$$[u](\zeta)\nu_t(\zeta)+[f](\zeta)\cdot\nu_x(\zeta)=0,$$
where $[u]=u^+-u^-$ and $[f]=f(u^+)-f(u^-)$.

In one space dimension, for a graph $x=s(t)$ with minus side $x<s(t)$ and plus
side $x>s(t)$, $\nu=(-s'(t),1)/\sqrt{1+s'(t)^2}$, so the condition is
$s'(t)[u](t)=[f](t)$ at every graph point. If $[u]\ne0$ in one dimension, then
$s'=[f]/[u]$; if $[u]=0$, then $[f]=0$ and the relation is $0=0$, with no speed
constraint.

Let $n\ge1$, $T>0$, $f\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^n)$, and
$\Pi_T=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$. The unknown and initial datum are equivalence
classes $[u]\in L^\infty(\Pi_T)$ and
$[u_0]\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, where
equality is Lebesgue-a.e. ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).

For $k\in\mathbb R$ define the **Kruzhkov entropy pair**
$$\eta_k(s)=|s-k|,\qquad q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)\bigl(f(s)-f(k)\bigr),$$
with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then $\eta_k$ is convex
and $q_k'=\eta_k'f'$ almost everywhere, so $(\eta_k,q_k)$ is a locally Lipschitz convex
entropy--entropy flux pair ([[def-convex-entropy-entropy-flux-pair]]).

The class $[u]$ is a **Kruzhkov entropy solution** of
$u_t+\operatorname{div}_x f(u)=0$ with initial trace $[u_0]$ if:

(i) for every $k\in\mathbb R$ and every nonnegative
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Pi_T)$,
$$\int_{\Pi_T}\bigl(\eta_k(u)\,\varphi_t+q_k(u)\cdot\nabla_x\varphi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\ge0,$$
that is, $\partial_t\eta_k(u)+\operatorname{div}_x q_k(u)\le0$ in
$\mathcal D'(\Pi_T)$; and

(ii) for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{0<t<\min\{\delta,T\}}\int_K|u(t,x)-u_0(x)|\,dx=0.$$

The integral in (i) is independent of the representative because its integrand
is unchanged almost everywhere. For (ii), Fubini's theorem gives locally
integrable spatial sections for almost every $t$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the
displayed slice integral is defined for those times and its essential supremum
ignores the exceptional null set. If $u$ or $u_0$ is changed on a null set in
its respective space, Fubini's theorem shows that the slice-integral function
changes only for a null set of times, so the trace condition is well defined on
the equivalence classes: this is the **strong local $L^1$ initial trace**.

Taking $k$ above and below the essential range of $u$ makes $\eta_k$ equal
$k-u$ and $u-k$, whose $t$- and $x$-derivatives cancel the constant terms
against compactly supported test functions, so the entropy inequalities imply
the weak conservation law of
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]] tested
against nonnegative test functions, hence by linearity against all test
functions.

To recover the Cauchy boundary term, apply the interior weak identity to
$\varphi(t,x)\zeta(t/\delta)$, where $\zeta$ is smooth and nondecreasing,
$\zeta=0$ on $(-\infty,1/2]$ and $\zeta=1$ on $[1,\infty)$.
For $\delta>0$ this product is supported away from $t=0$, so it is
an admissible interior test. The term containing $\zeta'/\delta$
converges to $\int u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx$ by (ii), while the other terms
converge on the compact support. This proves the full weak formulation with
initial datum $u_0$, rather than only its interior equation.

Let $u$ be an almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable functions on
$\mathbb R$ with $u\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$,
using the quotient convention of
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], the essentially bounded
class of [[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]], and the local integrability
convention of [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]. For $h>0$ define
$$D_hu(x):=u(x+h)-u(x),\qquad \operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u):=\sup_{h>0}\frac1h\int_{\mathbb R}|D_hu(x)|\,dx,$$
where the integral may be $+\infty$. The **bounded BV class on the line**
$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ consists of those classes for which
$\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u)<\infty$; we write
$\operatorname{TV}(u):=\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u)$.

This translation-variation convention is the standard one-dimensional BV
seminorm on bounded locally integrable classes. It is unchanged by modifying
$u$ on a null set, because each translate of a null set is null. It does not
require $u\in L^1(\mathbb R)$: every bounded constant function belongs to
$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and has variation $0$.

derivations.claim: The initial cell averages are $U_j^0=1$ for $j<0$ and $U_j^0=-1$ for $j\ge0$. Same-state faces have flux $1/2$ by [F1], and the only mixed face has pair $(1,-1)$ and flux $\max\{1,1\}/2=1/2$. Thus every face flux equals $1/2$.

Every cell's left and right fluxes are both $1/2$, so the conservative update leaves every $U_j^n$ unchanged. Induction in $n$ proves that both reconstructions equal the stationary step function almost everywhere for every $m$; in particular they converge strongly locally to it.

The stationary profile is a bounded weak solution: for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$, its time term satisfies $\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R}u\varphi_t\,dx\,dt=-\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx$, while $f_B(u)=1/2$ almost everywhere and hence $\int_{\mathbb R}f_B(u)\varphi_x\,dx=0$ at each time. This is exactly the weak identity of [F3].

Fix $k\in\mathbb R$. The entropy flux traces are $q_k(1)$ on the left and $q_k(-1)$ on the right. If $k\le-1$ or $k\ge1$, both states lie on the same side of $k$ and these fluxes are equal because $f_B(1)=f_B(-1)$. If $-1<k<1$, then $q_k(1)=\frac{1-k^2}{2},\qquad q_k(-1)=-\frac{1-k^2}{2},\qquad q_k(1)-q_k(-1)=1-k^2\ge0.$ For any nonnegative interior test $\varphi$, the time term $\int|u-k|\varphi_t$ vanishes because $u$ is stationary. Integration on the two half-lines gives $\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R}q_k(u)\varphi_x\,dx\,dt=(q_k(1)-q_k(-1))\int_0^T\varphi(0,t)\,dt\ge0.$ The initial trace is exactly $u_0$, so [F5] shows the stationary shock is a Kruzhkov entropy solution.

The left and right traces are $u_L=1$ and $u_R=-1$. By [F4], the shock speed is $s=\frac{f_B(-1)-f_B(1)}{-1-1}=\frac{1/2-1/2}{-2}=0,$ which agrees with the stationary interface. The Rankine–Hugoniot supplier applies because step 3.1 verified the weak identity and the traces are distinct.

The translation variation of the datum is $2$: for $h>0$, $u_0(x+h)-u_0(x)$ is nonzero only on $(-h,0)$, where its absolute value is $2$, so $\int|u_0(x+h)-u_0(x)|dx=2h$. The ratio is $\tau_m/h_m=1/4$, and the flux bounds $L_1=L_2=1$ from [F2] give $\lambda(L_1+L_2)=1/2\le1$. Thus the hypotheses of the main convergence theorem in [F2] hold; since the exact reconstruction is the entropy solution from step 3.2, it is the unique limit. No global $L^1$ assertion is made because the two tails are nonzero.
